##  · DOC1-packages — userland/packages.md: the user side of packages

Status: **open** · Assigned to: Architect · Revision: 3

### Userland writer · Question

Event: `98d948125f60c691ed5a70a1eb418442` · 2026-09-26T08:01:42Z

> M5 (persist, install, share): `pkg add`, `use`, `gc`; trust lists; profiles. Draft: a signed ustar plus strict-JSON manifest (domain redoubt.pkg.v1), installed under /system/pkgs/<principal>/<name>-<version>-<hash>/ which only the steward writes; profile and trust list are steward records; installing from a trusted signer needs no approval, adding a key is a high-stakes approval; upgrade is per package, `use` flips a record. Undecided: (a) is `pkg` a shell command talking to the pkg server, or the steward; (b) how .beam code in a package is loaded (the profile's directories on the VM's code path through Platform::load_module); (c) whether a principal can remove a key from its trust list without approval. RECOMMENDATION: (a) a Redoubt.Pkg module and `pkg` command over the pkg server, which asks the steward for grants; (b) yes: load_module reads only the profile's package directories, never the session's writable namespace; (c) removal needs no approval (it only narrows). Until answered the page lists these under Open.

### Architect · Answer

Event: `66d3691c7bc74bb0d834344243216953` · 2026-09-26T08:07:35Z

> Architect ruling, servers/pkg.md and userland/packages.md, M5 (persist, install, share). All three are adopted; (a) is sharpened because pkg parses hostile archives, and (b) and (c) get a detail each. Nothing stays Open.
> 
> (a) ADOPTED, with the authority split made explicit. There is a Redoubt.Pkg module and a `pkg` command, and they talk to the pkg server, as the brief's server list has it.
> - pkg does the parsing, so the steward never parses an archive. This is the same principle as 'init and the steward copy bytes; they never parse an ELF'.
> - Verify before parse. pkg checks the signature over the whole archive (the redoubt.pkg.v1 preimage, with the one shared verifier that boot and updates use) against the INSTALLING principal's trust list, before it reads a single tar header or manifest byte. An archive not signed by a trusted key never reaches the parser.
> - Containment of the parser. Keys on one principal's trust list can still sign a hostile archive. So the steward starts pkg per principal (per install), holding a write handle to that principal's package directory only, /system/pkgs/<principal>/, plus the archive it was handed. A parser bug then reaches only that principal's own packages, never another's.
> - This refines the legacy 'a directory only the steward writes'. Only the steward-started pkg instance for that principal writes it, and nothing a session holds does.
> - The steward keeps the authority. The profile, `use` records, trust lists and the grants a manifest requests are steward records. The grants are attenuated from the principal's own capabilities at install or run time, as settled. pkg asks the steward to record; it never holds grant authority itself.
> 
> (b) ADOPTED. Platform::load_module resolves module names only from the system bundle and the profile's package directories, through read-only handles, never the session's writable namespace. This is settled (legacy PACKAGES). Two additions:
> 1. No shadowing. A package may not define a module the system bundle defines, since Erlang's sticky-module idea applies. Two packages in one profile may not define the same module. pkg refuses the first case at install and the steward refuses the second at `use`, and the system bundle always resolves first.
> 2. Scope. The rule is about implicit code-path loading. A session that explicitly compiles or loads code itself (Code.compile_string, Code.require_file on its own files) is running code within its own authority. That is allowed and settled, and the page says so, so nobody mistakes the code-path rule for a wall against one's own code.
> 
> (c) ADOPTED. Removing a key from one's own trust list needs no approval, because it only narrows. It is audited. The effects are stated:
> - New launches and loads of that key's packages are refused at once.
> - The steward lists the principal's running processes whose recorded signer is that key, and stops them by destroying their budgets. This is the settled 'key compromise is containable'.
> - `use` records are never silently switched to another version or signer. A package left without a trusted signer is simply unusable until the principal chooses.
> - The system key is not on any trust list and cannot be removed; system code is trusted by the bundle's verification, not by a list.
> 
> TESTS for M5:
> - an unsigned or untrusted archive is refused before any parse (a fuzz corpus confirms the parser is never reached);
> - a hostile archive signed by a trusted key cannot write outside its principal's package directory;
> - a module named like a system module is refused;
> - a .beam planted in the session's home is never loaded by name;
> - removing a key stops that signer's running processes and leaves `use` records unchanged.

### Architect · Progress

Event: `1a143e098a096adc4495539c9654599f` · 2026-09-26T08:07:35Z

> cc: DOC1-packages answered, and nothing stays Open.
> (a) `pkg` goes through the pkg server. The signature is verified against the installer's trust list before any parse. The steward starts pkg per principal, holding a write handle only to /system/pkgs/<principal>/, so a parser bug reaches only that principal's own packages. The steward keeps the profile, trust and grant records.
> (b) load_module uses only the system bundle and the profile's package directories. There is no shadowing of system modules or between packages; explicit self-loaded code is within own authority.
> (c) Key removal needs no approval and is audited. It stops that signer's running processes and never silently switches `use` records. The system key is not removable.
